newsitem.title: USA: Texas separatists keep besieging police waiting.
newsitem.headline: Texas separatists keep besieging police waiting.

text.p: Elite police units waited patiently on Thursday in the hope that armed Texas separatists would break their silence and renew negotiations to end a five-day standoff in west Texas.

Richard McLaren, leader of the self-styled Republic of Texas, stopped answering telephone calls and faxes late on Tuesday just as state government officials and even McLaren's own lawyer thought they were close to a peaceful solution.

Officials said they had no idea whether he was having problems with his phone lines or other equipment or whether he and the other 12 Republic members holed up in their tin-wall compound were deliberately cutting off communication.
"We thought we had open dialogue with him and then, kerplunk, the wheel fell off," Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox told reporters. "We don't know why."
"Maybe the raccoons have eaten through the telephone line," quipped McLaren's attorney, Terence O'Rourke, as he tried to put a positive spin on his client's silence.

Police tried to restart talks by rumbling up to the compound in a 13-ton armoured personnel carrier to drop off a "diplomatic pouch" with messages from police and O'Rourke asking McLaren to call or send back his response in the pouch.

There had been no reply by midnight on Wednesday so police planned to repeat the operation Thursday. Cox and O'Rourke said negotiators had been on the verge of cutting a deal with the Republic members, who believe Texas is an independent nation and that they form its provisional government.

Under the deal, McLaren and his wife were to be given an opportunity to present before a federal magistrate their argument that the 1845 annexation of Texas by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836.

Electrical power was cut to McLaren's compound in the Davis Mountains of west Texas and police, backed by dozens of local, state and federal officers, two armoured personnel carrriers and nine bloodhounds, have the compound surrounded.
But Cox said they were not planning an armed assault to arrest McLaren and five others who face felony criminal charges with penalties of up to 99 years in prison."
"We are not interested in hurting anyone," Cox said. "Our bottom line here is to get a peaceful solution."

But many local residents, angered by the patient handling of Mclaren, want a quick solution and some believe violence may be necessary. "I think they should go in and kill him. I know that sounds mean but they been pushing people around long enough," said Beverly Clark, a store owner in this quaint resort town of 1,200 people.
